Let $m\geq0$ be a scalar rest energy in joules, and let $p_1,p_2,k_1,k_2$ be the incoming and outgoing scattering vectors on the positive $m$-shell of [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]], so each $(E,\mathbf q)$ satisfies $E=\sqrt{|\mathbf q|^2+m^2}>0$. Require $p_1+p_2=k_1+k_2=P$ and $s=h(P,P)>4m^2$, with $h$ as in [[def-qft-example-data]]. Evaluate the coefficient map in a center-of-momentum frame $\Lambda P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$ as defined in [[lem-qft-example-two-body-phase-space]]. For one scalar initial label of weight $1$ and one specified final channel, take the dimensionless real quartic tree amplitude $\mathcal A=-\lambda$. The coefficient map of [[lem-qft-example-two-body-phase-space]] gives
$$\frac{d\sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}}{d\Omega} =\frac{\lambda^2(\hbar c)^2}{128\pi^2s}, \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}=\frac{\lambda^2(\hbar c)^2}{32\pi s}$$
for identical final scalars integrated over the full labeled sphere. For distinguishable final scalars the two coefficients are twice these values.

For a parent at rest, $P_0=(\mathsf M_0,\mathbf0)$ with energy $\mathsf M_0>2m$, decaying through a specified single channel to two identical scalars on the positive $m$-shell whose total four-vector is $P_0$, under a constant amplitude $G_E$ in joules, the rate coefficient is
$$\Gamma_{\mathrm{coeff}} =\frac{|G_E|^2}{32\pi\hbar\mathsf M_0} \sqrt{1-\frac{4m^2}{\mathsf M_0^2}}.$$
This result concerns the defined formal coefficients. It does not assert an exact exponential survival law.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], and use [[def-qft-example-data]] and [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. Write
$$\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M}=\{(E,\mathbf q)\in(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^3:E=\sqrt{|\mathbf q|^2+\mathsf M^2}\}$$
for the positive shell in that Definition, and $C_+=\{(E,\mathbf q)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3:E\geq|\mathbf q|\}$ for the closed future cone of $h=(+,-,-,-)$. A proper orthochronous linear $h$-Lorentz map is a real linear $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda^Th\Lambda=h$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and $\Lambda(C_+)=C_+$. For energy four-vectors on these positive shells, the shell measure $\nu_{\mathsf M}$ defined there is invariant under every such map. Let $\mathsf M_1,\mathsf M_2\geq0$, let $P$ be future timelike, meaning $P^0>0$ and $h(P,P)>0$, set $s=h(P,P)>(\mathsf M_1+\mathsf M_2)^2$, and write $E_i(r)=\sqrt{r^2+\mathsf M_i^2}$. Let $f$ be a nonnegative Borel function on $\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_1}\times\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_2}$. For a proper orthochronous $h$-Lorentz map $\Lambda_P$ with $\Lambda_P P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$, define $\Phi_{2,P}$ as the pushforward of the angular measure $\Phi_2$ from that Definition under
$$\mathbf n\longmapsto\left(\Lambda_P^{-1}(E_1^*,k_*\mathbf n),\Lambda_P^{-1}(E_2^*,-k_*\mathbf n)\right),$$
where $E_i^*$ and $k_*$ are from [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. The proof below shows that $\Phi_{2,P}$ is independent of the choice of $\Lambda_P$; for $P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$ it is the pushforward $(\Psi_2)_\#\Phi_2$ under the center-of-momentum map $\Psi_2$ defined there. The standard two-body on-shell integral
$$(2\pi)^4\int d\nu_{\mathsf M_1}(k_1)d\nu_{\mathsf M_2}(k_2)\, \delta^{(4)}(P-k_1-k_2)\,f(k_1,k_2)$$
is interpreted by first evaluating the spatial delta in $k_2$, then the one-dimensional energy delta by the increasing radial change of variable $r\mapsto E_1(r)+E_2(r)$. Explicitly, for each fixed angular direction and nonnegative Borel radial function $g:(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]$, the radial action after spatial evaluation is $\int_0^\infty g(r)\delta(\sqrt{s}-E_1(r)-E_2(r))\,dr=g(k_*)/(d(E_1+E_2)/dr|_{k_*})$; this is the pushforward evaluation under that $C^1$ diffeomorphism, not a product of distributions. It equals $\int f\,d\Phi_{2,P}$. The threshold root is $k_*$ in that Definition, and
$$\Phi_{2,P}(\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_1}\times\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_2})=\Phi_2(S^2)=\frac{k_*}{4\pi\sqrt{s}}.$$
For equal rest energies $\mathsf M_1=\mathsf M_2=\mathsf M$, set $\beta=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/s}$; then $k_*=\sqrt{s}\beta/2$ and $\Phi_{2,P}(\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M}\times\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M})=\Phi_2(S^2)=\beta/(8\pi)$. For the scattering flux identities, take incoming $p_i=(E_i,\mathbf p_i)\in\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_{i,\mathrm{in}}}$, where $\mathsf M_{i,\mathrm{in}}\geq0$, and require $p_1+p_2=P$. A center-of-momentum map is a proper orthochronous $h$-Lorentz map $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$; write $\Lambda p_1=(E_1^*,\mathbf p_1^*)$ and define $p_*=|\mathbf p_1^*|$. The value is independent of the choice of $\Lambda$, since two such maps differ by a spatial rotation. Their invariant flux is $F=4p_*\sqrt{s}$. For equal incoming rest energies $\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}\geq0$ with $s\geq4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2$, define $\beta_{\mathrm{in}}=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2/s}$; then $p_*=\sqrt{s}\beta_{\mathrm{in}}/2$ and $F=2s\beta_{\mathrm{in}}$. For finite nonempty incoming and outgoing label sets, normalized initial weights, and the Borel amplitude family of the Definition, whenever $F>0$ the cross-section coefficient map gives
$$\frac{d\sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}}{d\Omega} =\frac{(\hbar c)^2}{64\pi^2s}\, \frac{k_*}{p_*}\, \frac{\overline{|\mathcal A|^2}}{S_f}.$$
For a parent at rest, represented by $P_0=(\mathsf M_0,\mathbf0)$ with $\mathsf M_0>2\mathsf M$, and two equal-rest-energy daughters on $\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M}$ with total four-vector $P_0$ and constant amplitude $G_E$ in joules, the rate coefficient is $|G_E|^2\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/\mathsf M_0^2}/(32\pi\hbar\mathsf M_0)$ when the daughters are identical. This is a coefficient calculation, not a claim of exponential survival.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

In $\mathbb R[X,t]/(t^2)$, the coefficient of $tX$ in $(mc^2+taX)^2$ is $2mc^2a$. The defining identity in the Statement sets this equal to $c^2$, so $a=1/(2m)$ since $m>0$. Substituting $K$ for $X$, the spin part of $K/(2m)$ is $-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B/(2m)=-(q/m)\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$.

Direct multiplication of the displayed $2\times2$ matrices gives $\sigma_i^2=I_2$, $\sigma_1\sigma_2=i\sigma_3$, $\sigma_2\sigma_3=i\sigma_1$, and $\sigma_3\sigma_1=i\sigma_2$; each reversed product has the opposite sign. Thus $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I_2+i\epsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$. Block multiplication gives $\alpha_i\alpha_j=\delta_{ij}I_4+i\epsilon_{ijk}\Sigma_k$, $\alpha_i\beta=-\beta\alpha_i$, and $\beta^2=I_4$. These fixed constant matrices commute with every $\pi_j$. The coefficient of the term linear in $q$ is $-(q/m)\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$. Let $m>0$ be a particle mass in kilograms, $q\in\mathbb R$ its charge in coulombs, and $A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ a smooth spatial vector potential with components in tesla-metres. Use standard Cartesian coordinates $x_i$ measured in metres and write $\partial_i:=\partial/\partial x_i$. Let $\epsilon_{ijk}$ be the alternating symbol with $\epsilon_{123}=1$, and sum repeated spatial indices from $1$ to $3$. Define $B_k(x)=\epsilon_{kij}\partial_iA_j(x)$ and $\mathbf B=(B_1,B_2,B_3):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$; its smooth components are in tesla.

Let $\mathcal C=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^4)$ be the common invariant test domain. In this item, “common core” refers only to this shared domain of the displayed differential expressions; no operator-theoretic core property for a closure is asserted. Define the dimensionless finite matrices
$$\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},$$
$$\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_i=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_i\\\sigma_i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \Sigma_i=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i,\sigma_i),$$

their time-dependent Hermitian interaction when present, a dimensionless
coupling parameter, an initial state, and an explicitly supplied finite
outcome measurement. A pure initial state is a vector $\psi\in\mathbb C^d$
with $\|\psi\|=1$; a mixed state is a matrix $\rho=\rho^*$ with

An exact regulated observable on this finite space is a specified Hermitian
matrix $O=O^*$ with a declared physical unit. The matrix and state are model
data; the measurement procedure and any physical rule assigning outcomes are
additional data. This definition does not say that an operator symbol by
itself is a detector outcome or probability.

A **finite probability law** on the declared outcome set
$\{1,\ldots,m\}$, $m\ge1$, is a vector $(p_1,\ldots,p_m)$ with
$p_a\ge0$ and $\sum_{a=1}^m p_a=1$. It is a mathematical type. Assigning that
law to a particular preparation and measurement is a separate physical
postulate. A prediction derived from an actually constructed regulated model
is conditional on those inputs and the adopted rule.

A **formal coefficient record** is a sequence $(c_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of
specified coefficients, sometimes displayed as the symbol
$\sum_{n\ge0}c_n\lambda^n$. Unless convergence and an evaluation map are
separately proved and adopted, the symbol records coefficients only: it is not
an evaluated function, exact probability, convergent perturbation series, or
error bound. A formal coefficient can be assigned a phenomenological meaning
only by a separate, model-specific physical adoption with its approximation
scope stated.

An **empirical estimate** is a source-reported number obtained by analyzing a
finite record of measurement outcomes under the stated preparation, apparatus,
calibration, sampling, and analysis conditions. Its reported uncertainty and
conditions travel with the estimate. It is not the exact model value, and it
does not prove the framework used to interpret it. The 2022 Fan et al. report
is an example of a source-reported electron magnetic-moment determination;
this definition supplies no numerical result, uncertainty reconstruction, or
new experimental claim.

Primitive and derived status is formulation-relative. In a selected regulated
model, the regulator, Hamiltonian data, coupling, initial state, and supplied

formal calculation, the specified masses, couplings, coefficient rules, and

In the natural-length variables of the Dirac definition, $\mathbf k=\mathbf p/(\hbar c)$, $\mu=M/(\hbar c)$, and $\omega=E/(\hbar c)$.

Let $\beta=\gamma^0$, $\alpha_j=\beta\gamma^j$, $\Sigma_j=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_j,\sigma_j)$, and $\gamma_5=i\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3$. Define $H_\pm=\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf p\pm\beta M$ and $P_\pm=(I_4+H_\pm/E)/2$. Each $P_\pm$ is a Hermitian rank-two projection. Choose orthonormal bases $\xi_{\pm,1},\xi_{\pm,2}$ of their ranges and put $u_s=\sqrt{2E}\xi_{+,s}$ and $v_s=\sqrt{2E}\xi_{-,s}$ for $s=1,2$. With $\bar z=z^\dagger\beta$ and $\not p=\gamma^0E-\sum_j\gamma^jp_j$, the following hold:

$$\operatorname{Tr}I_4=4,\quad \operatorname{Tr}\gamma^a=0,\quad \operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^a\gamma^b)=4h^{ab},\quad \operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma^c)=0,$$

$$\operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma^c\gamma^d) =4(h^{ab}h^{cd}-h^{ac}h^{bd}+h^{ad}h^{bc}), \qquad \sum_s u_s\bar u_s=\not p+M,\quad \sum_s v_s\bar v_s=\not p-M.$$

The columns satisfy $(\not p-M)u_s=0$ and $(\not p+M)v_s=0$. For all $x,y\in\mathbb C^4$, complex conjugation of a Dirac current is $\overline{\bar x\gamma^a y}=\bar y\gamma^a x$. The Countable Choice hypothesis written in the current draft [[def-qft-dirac-projections]] is retained as a supplier assumption; this finite-dimensional proof makes no additional choice use.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], and use [[def-qft-example-data]] and [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. Write
$$\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M}=\{(E,\mathbf q)\in(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^3:E=\sqrt{|\mathbf q|^2+\mathsf M^2}\}$$
for the positive shell in that Definition, and $C_+=\{(E,\mathbf q)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3:E\geq|\mathbf q|\}$ for the closed future cone of $h=(+,-,-,-)$. A proper orthochronous linear $h$-Lorentz map is a real linear $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda^Th\Lambda=h$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and $\Lambda(C_+)=C_+$. For energy four-vectors on these positive shells, the shell measure $\nu_{\mathsf M}$ defined there is invariant under every such map. Let $\mathsf M_1,\mathsf M_2\geq0$, let $P$ be future timelike, meaning $P^0>0$ and $h(P,P)>0$, set $s=h(P,P)>(\mathsf M_1+\mathsf M_2)^2$, and write $E_i(r)=\sqrt{r^2+\mathsf M_i^2}$. Let $f$ be a nonnegative Borel function on $\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_1}\times\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_2}$. For a proper orthochronous $h$-Lorentz map $\Lambda_P$ with $\Lambda_P P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$, define $\Phi_{2,P}$ as the pushforward of the angular measure $\Phi_2$ from that Definition under
$$\mathbf n\longmapsto\left(\Lambda_P^{-1}(E_1^*,k_*\mathbf n),\Lambda_P^{-1}(E_2^*,-k_*\mathbf n)\right),$$
where $E_i^*$ and $k_*$ are from [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. The proof below shows that $\Phi_{2,P}$ is independent of the choice of $\Lambda_P$; for $P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$ it is the pushforward $(\Psi_2)_\#\Phi_2$ under the center-of-momentum map $\Psi_2$ defined there. The standard two-body on-shell integral
$$(2\pi)^4\int d\nu_{\mathsf M_1}(k_1)d\nu_{\mathsf M_2}(k_2)\, \delta^{(4)}(P-k_1-k_2)\,f(k_1,k_2)$$
is interpreted by first evaluating the spatial delta in $k_2$, then the one-dimensional energy delta by the increasing radial change of variable $r\mapsto E_1(r)+E_2(r)$. Explicitly, for each fixed angular direction and nonnegative Borel radial function $g:(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]$, the radial action after spatial evaluation is $\int_0^\infty g(r)\delta(\sqrt{s}-E_1(r)-E_2(r))\,dr=g(k_*)/(d(E_1+E_2)/dr|_{k_*})$; this is the pushforward evaluation under that $C^1$ diffeomorphism, not a product of distributions. It equals $\int f\,d\Phi_{2,P}$. The threshold root is $k_*$ in that Definition, and
$$\Phi_{2,P}(\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_1}\times\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_2})=\Phi_2(S^2)=\frac{k_*}{4\pi\sqrt{s}}.$$
For equal rest energies $\mathsf M_1=\mathsf M_2=\mathsf M$, set $\beta=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/s}$; then $k_*=\sqrt{s}\beta/2$ and $\Phi_{2,P}(\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M}\times\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M})=\Phi_2(S^2)=\beta/(8\pi)$. For the scattering flux identities, take incoming $p_i=(E_i,\mathbf p_i)\in\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_{i,\mathrm{in}}}$, where $\mathsf M_{i,\mathrm{in}}\geq0$, and require $p_1+p_2=P$. A center-of-momentum map is a proper orthochronous $h$-Lorentz map $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$; write $\Lambda p_1=(E_1^*,\mathbf p_1^*)$ and define $p_*=|\mathbf p_1^*|$. The value is independent of the choice of $\Lambda$, since two such maps differ by a spatial rotation. Their invariant flux is $F=4p_*\sqrt{s}$. For equal incoming rest energies $\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}\geq0$ with $s\geq4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2$, define $\beta_{\mathrm{in}}=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2/s}$; then $p_*=\sqrt{s}\beta_{\mathrm{in}}/2$ and $F=2s\beta_{\mathrm{in}}$. For finite nonempty incoming and outgoing label sets, normalized initial weights, and the Borel amplitude family of the Definition, whenever $F>0$ the cross-section coefficient map gives
$$\frac{d\sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}}{d\Omega} =\frac{(\hbar c)^2}{64\pi^2s}\, \frac{k_*}{p_*}\, \frac{\overline{|\mathcal A|^2}}{S_f}.$$
For a parent at rest, represented by $P_0=(\mathsf M_0,\mathbf0)$ with $\mathsf M_0>2\mathsf M$, and two equal-rest-energy daughters on $\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M}$ with total four-vector $P_0$ and constant amplitude $G_E$ in joules, the rate coefficient is $|G_E|^2\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/\mathsf M_0^2}/(32\pi\hbar\mathsf M_0)$ when the daughters are identical. This is a coefficient calculation, not a claim of exponential survival.

The coefficient map of [[lem-qft-example-two-body-phase-space]] gives

This result concerns the defined formal coefficients. It does not assert an exact exponential survival law.

$$\phi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R),\qquad \mathbf A\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R^3),\qquad \psi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb C^4),\qquad \chi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R).$$
Define the lower-potential component maps $A_a:U\to\mathbb R$ by $A_0=-\phi/c$ and $A_j=\mathbf A_j$; collectively $(A_a)$ is the real covector potential in this chart. In fixed SI units, $\phi$ is in volts, each $A_a$ is in $\mathrm{T\,m}$, $\psi$ is assigned field dimension $\mathrm m^{-3/2}$, and $\chi$ is in webers; these unit labels accompany the maps and do not identify $q$ with a measured charge. $$A_a=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A),$$

In a named inertial chart, let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ be the
electromagnetic potential when one is supplied, with components in
$\mathrm{T\,m}$ under [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]. Define the canonical potential and

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have engineering dimensions $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\mathrm m^{-2}$,
respectively. With the metric-lowered potential
$A_{{\rm SI},a}=\eta_{ab}A^b_{\rm SI}$, the potential component convention is
$A_{{\rm SI},0}=-\varphi/c$ and $A_{{\rm SI},i}=A_i$. The covariant derivative
in the selected QED model is

$$D_a:=\partial_a-iq_{\rm n}a_a =\partial_a-\frac{iq_{\rm SI}}{\hbar}A_{{\rm SI},a},$$

since $q_{\rm n}a_a=q_{\rm SI}A_{{\rm SI},a}/\hbar$. Both terms in $D_a$
have unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. If the SI gauge function $\chi$ has unit
$\mathrm{Wb}=\mathrm{T\,m^2}$, then $q_{\rm SI}\chi/\hbar$ is dimensionless;
the corresponding natural gauge function
$\lambda=\chi/\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}$ is dimensionless and

Let $m>0$ be a particle mass in kilograms, $q\in\mathbb R$ its charge in coulombs, and $A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ a smooth spatial vector potential with components in tesla-metres. Use standard Cartesian coordinates $x_i$ measured in metres and write $\partial_i:=\partial/\partial x_i$. Let $\epsilon_{ijk}$ be the alternating symbol with $\epsilon_{123}=1$, and sum repeated spatial indices from $1$ to $3$. Define $B_k(x)=\epsilon_{kij}\partial_iA_j(x)$ and $\mathbf B=(B_1,B_2,B_3):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$; its smooth components are in tesla.

Let $\mathcal C=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^4)$ be the common invariant test domain. In this item, “common core” refers only to this shared domain of the displayed differential expressions; no operator-theoretic core property for a closure is asserted. Define the dimensionless finite matrices
$$\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},$$
$$\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_i=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_i\\\sigma_i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \Sigma_i=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i,\sigma_i),$$
and use $\hbar,c$ of [[def-qft-example-data]]. On $\mathcal C$, define
$$\pi_i\psi=-i\hbar\partial_i\psi-qA_i\psi,\qquad H_D\psi=c\sum_{i=1}^3\alpha_i\pi_i\psi+\beta mc^2\psi.$$
These maps preserve $\mathcal C$. The components $\pi_i$ have units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$ and $H_D$ has units joules. Define the operator expressions
$$\boldsymbol\pi^2\psi:=\sum_{i=1}^3\pi_i(\pi_i\psi),\qquad (\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B)\psi:=\sum_{i=1}^3\Sigma_iB_i\psi.$$
Here $[\pi_i,\pi_j]:=\pi_i\circ\pi_j-\pi_j\circ\pi_i$, and $H_D^2$ denotes composition on $\mathcal C$. On $\mathcal C$, the identities are
$$[\pi_i,\pi_j]=iq\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}B_k,\qquad H_D^2=m^2c^4I_4+c^2(\boldsymbol\pi^2-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B).$$
The operator $K:=\boldsymbol\pi^2-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B$ maps $\mathcal C$ to itself and has units $(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}})^2$.

For commuting formal indeterminates $t,X$ over $\mathbb R$, define the first-order square-root coefficient $a$ by
$$(mc^2+taX)^2\equiv m^2c^4+tc^2X\pmod{t^2}.$$
Comparing the coefficient of $tX$ gives $a=1/(2m)$; substituting $K$ for $X$ gives the formal first-degree correction $K/(2m)$, with no operator square-root assertion. Its spin term is $-(q/m)\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$, where $S_i=\hbar\Sigma_i/2$, $\mathbf S=(S_1,S_2,S_3)$, and $(\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B)\psi:=\sum_{i=1}^3S_iB_i\psi$. The magnetic-moment dot product below uses the same componentwise sum convention.

Under the coefficient convention $H_{\mathrm{mag}}=-\boldsymbol\mu_{\mathrm{mag}}\cdot\mathbf B$ and $\boldsymbol\mu_{\mathrm{mag}}=g_s(q/(2m))\mathbf S$, equality of the formal coefficients as a linear function of $q$ gives $g_s=2$ for the minimal tree-level term. Here $H_{\mathrm{mag}}$ has units joules and $\boldsymbol\mu_{\mathrm{mag}}$ has units $\mathrm{A\,m^2}$. No magnetic self-adjoint closure, full spectrum, operator square-root theorem, radiative correction, or empirical prediction is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], the mathematical scalar shell conventions of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and the second-variable-linear Hilbert pairing of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. In the fixed inertial coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] on the affine Minkowski model [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; these coordinates have length units under [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. The parameter $\mu\ge0$ and momentum coordinate $\mathbf k$ have inverse-length units, and $\omega(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same units. The parameter is not identified here with a physical rest mass. Matrix $h_D$ has inverse-length units; the dimensionless spin matrices have no physical unit assignment in this mathematical item.

Use the Pauli matrices $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. On $\mathbb C^4=\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C^2$, define
$$\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \gamma^0=\beta,\qquad \gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j.$$
For a spinor column $z\in\mathbb C^4$, its Dirac adjoint is $\bar z=z^\dagger\beta$. The Clifford contraction is $\Gamma(p):=\gamma^0p^0-\sum_{j=1}^3\gamma^jp_j$; this contraction uses the effective matrix $-\eta$ in the relation $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$.

Let $\mathcal H_D$ be the space of measurable functions $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^4$, modulo equality almost everywhere, with
$$\|u\|^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(\mathbf k)^\dagger u(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}<\infty,$$
and pairing $\langle u,v\rangle=\int u(\mathbf k)^\dagger v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k/(2\pi)^3$. Define the measurable matrix $h_D(\mathbf k)=\sum_j\alpha_j k_j+\beta\mu$ and its maximal multiplication operator with domain $D(h_D)=\{u\in\mathcal H_D:h_Du\in\mathcal H_D\}$. For $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix fields
$$P_\pm(\mathbf k)=\frac12\left(I_4\pm\frac{h_D(\mathbf k)}{\omega(\mathbf k)}\right).$$
When $\mu=0$ at $\mathbf k=0$, set $P_+(0)=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,0)$ and $P_-(0)=\operatorname{diag}(0,I_2)$. These are complementary rank-two orthogonal projections; the value at this Lebesgue-null point does not change their multiplication operators. Write $M_{P_\pm}$ for their maximal multiplication operators and $\mathcal H_\pm=\operatorname{ran}M_{P_\pm}$. The companion matrix lemma on this page proves these are bounded orthogonal projections with closed ranges. The conjugate Hilbert space $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ has vectors $\bar u$, scalar multiplication $z\bar u=\overline{\bar z u}$, and pairing $\langle\bar u,\bar v\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle$.

Use the sine and cosine definitions of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]. For a length-coordinate increment $t\in\mathbb R$ and $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix multiplier
$$W_D(t,\mathbf k)=\cos(\omega t)I_4+i\frac{\sin(\omega t)}{\omega}h_D(\mathbf k).$$
At the massless apex set $W_D(t,0)=I_4$. Its unitarity, group law and generator identity are proved by the companion matrix lemma on this page.

The symbols $P_+$ and $P_-$ designate the positive- and negative-energy matrix formulas for this fixed free Dirac operator. This is purely mathematical data; no physical spin-statistics postulate or empirical assertion is included.

These are conventions for constructed and formal calculations in this page pair. They are not empirical claims, physical postulates, or existence claims about an interacting continuum theory.

Work on a nonempty open coordinate region $U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, with coordinates $x^0=ct,x^1,x^2,x^3$ in metres and $\partial_a=\partial/\partial x^a$ for $a\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. Use the geometric spacetime metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and the time coordinate $x^0=ct$ in metres. For Clifford algebra and momentum contraction use the separate algebraic metric $h=-\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$; a slash or a square of an energy four-vector uses $h$, never $\eta$.

A physical energy four-vector is $p=(E,c\mathbf p_{\rm phys})$, with each component in joules. Write $M=mc^2$ for rest energy in joules and $p^2=h(p,p)=E^2-c^2|\mathbf p_{\rm phys}|^2$. For two such vectors, $s=(p_1+p_2)^2$ is in $\mathrm J^2$. Natural momentum coordinates are the energy-vector components divided by $\hbar c$, in $\mathrm m^{-1}$; they are not substituted into SI formulas without restoring this factor. Here $m\ge0$ is a mass parameter in kilograms, so $\mu=mc/\hbar$ is in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. The natural-unit field convention below concerns smooth test fields, not pointwise quantum operators. A real scalar field is a map $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$; a Dirac test field is $\Psi\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb C^4)$. Fix dimensionless matrices $\gamma^a\in M_4(\mathbb C)$ satisfying $\gamma^a\gamma^b+\gamma^b\gamma^a=2h^{ab}I_4$, and put $\overline\Psi=\Psi^\dagger\gamma^0$. Adopt dimensionless action normalizations with kinetic terms $\tfrac12\int_U h^{ab}(\partial_a\varphi)(\partial_b\varphi)\,d^4x$ and $\int_U i\overline\Psi\gamma^a\partial_a\Psi\,d^4x$, summing repeated indices from $0$ to $3$. The coefficients are dimensionless and introduce no additional length scale. These conventions assign $[\varphi]=\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $[\Psi]=\mathrm m^{-3/2}$: the integrands have length degrees $2[\varphi]-2$ and $2[\Psi]-1$, while $d^4x$ has degree $4$. No dynamics or continuum existence assertion is adopted.

Take SI $e>0$ in coulombs, $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, $c>0$ in metres per second, $\mu_0>0$ in $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{kg\,m\,C^{-2}}$, and $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$. Define
$$\alpha=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0\hbar c},\qquad g=e\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}=\sqrt{4\pi\alpha}>0.$$
Here $g$ is a dimensionless coupling. It is not the metric and not a gyromagnetic factor.

For gauge notation take $\phi\in C^1(U;\mathbb R)$ in volts and $\mathbf A\in C^1(U;\mathbb R^3)$ in tesla-metres. Write $A_{\rm lower}=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A)$ for the components of the real one-form $A=\sum_{a=0}^3 A_a\,dx^a$, so every $A_a$ is in tesla-metres. Take $\chi\in C^2(U;\mathbb R)$ in webers and a charged test field $\psi\in C^1(U;\mathbb C^N)$, where $N\ge1$ is fixed. With a constant real charge parameter $q$ in coulombs, define $D_a\psi=\partial_a\psi-iqA_a\psi/\hbar$ componentwise. The transformed fields are again $C^1$, with $d\chi=\sum_a(\partial_a\chi)dx^a$. In operator notation the conventions are
$$D_a=\partial_a-\frac{iqA_a}{\hbar},\qquad \psi\mapsto e^{iq\chi/\hbar}\psi,\qquad A\mapsto A+d\chi.$$
For the electron parameter use $q=-e$. The equivalent natural-unit coordinates are $A_{\rm nat}=A_{\rm SI}/\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}$ and $q_{\rm nat}=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$.

Finite-matrix examples act on $\mathbb C^d$ with the operator norm. For Hilbert spaces, use the first-variable-linear pairing $(u,v)_1=v^\dagger u$; a displayed coordinate contraction $u^\dagger v$ is second-variable-linear and equals $\overline{(u,v)_1}$. Thus norms, traces, and modulus-squared amplitudes agree under conversion, although the unsquared pairing is conjugated. No amplitude is assigned a probability by these conventions.

Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and an inertial
chart of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinates
$x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres, and coordinate time $t$ in seconds as in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Greek spacetime indices run
from $0$ to $3$; spatial indices run from $1$ to $3$ and are contracted with
the Euclidean spatial metric. The coordinates $x^a$ have unit metre and
$\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

The positive constants $c$, $h$ and $e_{\rm SI}$ have the exact SI defining
values; write $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. The magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ has SI unit
$\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ and is experimentally determined under the current SI;
no exact numerical value or current estimate for it is adopted. Put
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ when that symbol is used. These are SI
normalization inputs, not empirical claims about a selected QFT model.

For a species with rest mass $m_{\rm rest,SI}>0$ in kilograms define its
inverse-length mass parameter

$$\mu:=\frac{m_{\rm rest,SI}c}{\hbar}\quad[\mathrm m^{-1}].$$

For a spatial wave vector $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, with each component in
$\mathrm m^{-1}$ and the Euclidean norm, define
$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k):=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}\in\mathbb R_{>0}$, with
unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Here $\omega_\mu$ is the temporal wave number, not the
SI angular frequency; the corresponding SI angular frequency is
$c\omega_\mu$. Energy and momentum are $E=\hbar c\omega_\mu$ in joules and
$\mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. With
$p=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)\in\mathbb R^4$ and
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)\in\mathbb R^4$, the phase convention is

$$p\mathbin{\circ}x:=\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$

For a selected local action represented on a chart region
$\mathcal U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ by
$$\frac{S}{\hbar}=\int_{\mathcal U}\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}(x)\,d^4x,\quad d^4x:=dx^0dx^1dx^2dx^3,$$
the natural Lagrangian density $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}$ has unit
$\mathrm m^{-4}$. Since $x^0=ct$, the corresponding SI Lagrangian density is
$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{SI}}:=\hbar c\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}$ and has unit

Lagrangian density with the model's Hamiltonian energy density.

For canonical engineering dimensions in this four-dimensional normalization,
use the formal field symbols $\phi_{\rm n}$ and $\psi_{\rm n}$ in the selected
scalar and Dirac kinetic terms, assigning them length degrees $-1$ and
$-3/2$, respectively. These are the dimensions fixed by those free kinetic
terms, not exact scaling dimensions of interacting fields: anomalous
dimensions, when present, are separate quantities. These symbols do not
assert pointwise field maps or operator fields; a model supplies its field
space and regularity. Let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ and
$F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}$ use the component convention of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], namely
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, with
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$ only when a potential is
supplied. Define the normalized photon potential and field strength by

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have length degrees $-1$ and $-2$, respectively. The EM supplier is used
only for SI units and tensor components: no classical Maxwell equation,
Lorentz-force law, or classical-to-quantum identification is adopted here.

For any separately declared SI charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}$ in coulombs put

$$q_{\rm n}:=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}.$$

It is dimensionless. For the positive exact SI elementary charge use
$e_{\rm n}:=e_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$ and define the rationalized

measured, these formulas do not assign an exact numerical value to
$e_{\rm n}$ or $\alpha$. If the model uses minimal coupling, its convention is
$D_\mu=\partial_\mu-iq_{\rm n}a_\mu$; for an electron with
$q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$ this reads $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+ie_{\rm n}a_\mu$.
Bare, renormalized-at-scale, and measured effective charges are separately
labelled model parameters; applying the conversion to one label does not
identify it with either of the others or specify a running law.

In a supplied four-component spinor representation, let
$\gamma^a\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb C^4)$, $a=0,1,2,3$, be
dimensionless linear maps satisfying
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}:=\gamma^a\gamma^b+\gamma^b\gamma^a
=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$, where $I_4$ is the identity map. Set $\beta:=\gamma^0$
and $\alpha^i:=\beta\gamma^i$; then $\beta^2=I_4$ and
$\gamma^i=\beta\alpha^i$. For a supplied four-component spinor $\psi$ write

A supplied free Dirac model may use
$(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0$ for its model-supplied spinor field
$\psi$; that model supplies its field domain and regularity. The phase and
Clifford choices are conventions; this item proves no representation or field

If a selected model supplies a complex Hilbert space $\mathscr H$ as in
[[def-hilbert-space]], a complex-linear Hamiltonian operator
$H:D(H)\to\mathscr H$ with model-specified linear domain $D(H)\subseteq\mathscr H$
and SI energy unit joules, and an evolution family $U(t):\mathscr H\to\mathscr H$
for $t\in I\subseteq\mathbb R$ in seconds, the convention is
$U(t)=\exp(-itH/\hbar)$. Each $U(t)$ is a surjective complex-linear map
satisfying $\langle U(t)\xi,U(t)\zeta\rangle=\langle\xi,\zeta\rangle$
for all $\xi,\zeta\in\mathscr H$; write $U(t)^*:=U(t)^{-1}$. The exponent
is dimensionless because $\hbar$ has unit $\mathrm{J\,s}$. For any
model-supplied complex-linear operator $O:D(O)\to\mathscr H$, with specified
linear domain $D(O)\subseteq\mathscr H$, define its Heisenberg conjugate by
$$O_H(t):=U(t)^*O\,U(t),\quad
D(O_H(t)):=\{\xi\in\mathscr H:U(t)\xi\in D(O)\}.$$
The model supplies these domains and the evolution; this dictionary constructs
no Hamiltonian, evolution family, or field representation. Where a free-field
module uses an inner product linear in its second variable, convert to the
repository's first-variable-linear pairing by
$\langle u,v\rangle_{\rm FF}=(v,u)_{\rm root}$.

For precision about domains, let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space with
inner product linear in its first variable and let
$\mathscr D\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a dense complex linear subspace. A **weak operator-valued distribution
on the common domain $\mathscr D$** means a complex-linear assignment
$g\mapsto\Phi(g)$ for $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$, where each
$\Phi(g):\mathscr D\to\mathcal H$ is linear and, for every
$u,v\in\mathscr D$, the scalar map
$g\mapsto\langle\Phi(g)u,v\rangle$ is a continuous complex-linear functional

[[def-test-function-topology]], hence a distribution as in [[def-distribution]].
This definition gives no pointwise field $\Phi(x)$ and no product
$\Phi(x)\Phi(x)$; a product or extension needs a separate construction. It

and gauge-specific potential behavior must be supplied by a constructed
model. Test-function units can be chosen so a specified smeared observable is

derived only when their constructions supply the required domains and

Use the framework-local unit and domain dictionary of
[[def-qft-framework-units]] and the energy, SI/natural-unit, and finite-matrix
conventions of [[def-qft-example-data]]. A physical quantity is always typed
relative to the selected QFT formulation and its declared model data; its name
or units alone do not identify it with a quantity in another formulation.

For the **exact finite-regulator class** used on this page, the state space is
the finite-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^d$ for an integer
$d\ge1$. Model inputs include the selected Hermitian Hamiltonian matrices,
their time-dependent Hermitian interaction when present, a dimensionless
coupling parameter, an initial state, and an explicitly supplied finite
outcome measurement. A pure initial state is a vector $\psi\in\mathbb C^d$
with $\|\psi\|=1$; a mixed state is a matrix $\rho=\rho^*$ with

matrix $O=O^*$ with a declared physical unit. The matrix and state are model

$\{1,\ldots,m\}$, $m\ge1$, is a vector $(p_1,\ldots,p_m)$ with

law to a particular preparation and measurement is a separate physical

does not prove the framework used to interpret it. The 2022 Fan et al. report
is an example of a source-reported electron magnetic-moment determination;

Adopt a smooth local classical Maxwell–Dirac model on an open region of the
flat spacetime specified by [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Let $A_{{\rm SI},a}$
be a supplied real $C^\infty$ electromagnetic covector potential and let
$\psi:\!U\to\mathbb C^4$ be a $C^\infty$ commuting spinor field. The charge
$q_{\rm SI}$ and rest mass $m_{\rm SI}>0$ are model inputs; for the electron
take $q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$. Use the component, metric, Clifford, charge,
field-normalization, and unit conventions of
[[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]], [[def-qft-qed-physical-gauge-quantities]],
[[def-qft-framework-units]], and the electromagnetic suppliers of
[[post-qft-free-photon-model]]. In particular,
$D_a=\partial_a-iq_{\rm SI}A_{{\rm SI},a}/\hbar
=\partial_a-iq_{\rm n}a_a$ and $\mu=m_{\rm SI}c/\hbar$.

Adopt the local action density in natural normalization

$$\mathcal L_{\rm nat} =-\frac14 f_{ab}f^{ab} +\frac{i}{2}\bigl(\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\psi -(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\psi\bigr)-\mu\bar\psi\psi,$$

where $f_{ab}=\partial_a a_b-\partial_ba_a$ on the region where the
potential is supplied, $\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta$, and
$D_a\bar\psi=\partial_a\bar\psi+iq_{\rm n}a_a\bar\psi$. The physical action
is $S_{\rm cl}=\hbar\int_U\mathcal L_{\rm nat}\,d^4x$ with $x^0=ct$. For
compactly supported local variations this is the adopted classical
Maxwell–Dirac formulation; its Euler–Lagrange consequences are not postulated
as a proof in this item.

For a smooth gauge function $\chi$ in webers, the adopted local
transformation is
$A_{{\rm SI},a}\mapsto A_{{\rm SI},a}+\partial_a\chi$ and
$\psi\mapsto e^{iq_{\rm SI}\chi/\hbar}\psi$. It leaves $F=dA$ invariant and
makes $D_a\psi$ transform by the same phase. This is the covector form of the

The model adopts the separately specified free Dirac representation of

These are conventions for constructed and formal calculations in this page pair. They are not empirical claims, physical postulates, or existence claims about an interacting continuum theory.

Work on a nonempty open coordinate region $U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, with coordinates $x^0=ct,x^1,x^2,x^3$ in metres and $\partial_a=\partial/\partial x^a$ for $a\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. Use the geometric spacetime metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and the time coordinate $x^0=ct$ in metres. For Clifford algebra and momentum contraction use the separate algebraic metric $h=-\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$; a slash or a square of an energy four-vector uses $h$, never $\eta$.

A physical energy four-vector is $p=(E,c\mathbf p_{\rm phys})$, with each component in joules. Write $M=mc^2$ for rest energy in joules and $p^2=h(p,p)=E^2-c^2|\mathbf p_{\rm phys}|^2$. For two such vectors, $s=(p_1+p_2)^2$ is in $\mathrm J^2$. Natural momentum coordinates are the energy-vector components divided by $\hbar c$, in $\mathrm m^{-1}$; they are not substituted into SI formulas without restoring this factor. Here $m\ge0$ is a mass parameter in kilograms, so $\mu=mc/\hbar$ is in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. The natural-unit field convention below concerns smooth test fields, not pointwise quantum operators. A real scalar field is a map $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$; a Dirac test field is $\Psi\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb C^4)$. Fix dimensionless matrices $\gamma^a\in M_4(\mathbb C)$ satisfying $\gamma^a\gamma^b+\gamma^b\gamma^a=2h^{ab}I_4$, and put $\overline\Psi=\Psi^\dagger\gamma^0$. Adopt dimensionless action normalizations with kinetic terms $\tfrac12\int_U h^{ab}(\partial_a\varphi)(\partial_b\varphi)\,d^4x$ and $\int_U i\overline\Psi\gamma^a\partial_a\Psi\,d^4x$, summing repeated indices from $0$ to $3$. The coefficients are dimensionless and introduce no additional length scale. These conventions assign $[\varphi]=\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $[\Psi]=\mathrm m^{-3/2}$: the integrands have length degrees $2[\varphi]-2$ and $2[\Psi]-1$, while $d^4x$ has degree $4$. No dynamics or continuum existence assertion is adopted.

Take SI $e>0$ in coulombs, $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, $c>0$ in metres per second, $\mu_0>0$ in $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{kg\,m\,C^{-2}}$, and $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$. Define
$$\alpha=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0\hbar c},\qquad g=e\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}=\sqrt{4\pi\alpha}>0.$$
Here $g$ is a dimensionless coupling. It is not the metric and not a gyromagnetic factor.

For gauge notation take $\phi\in C^1(U;\mathbb R)$ in volts and $\mathbf A\in C^1(U;\mathbb R^3)$ in tesla-metres. Write $A_{\rm lower}=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A)$ for the components of the real one-form $A=\sum_{a=0}^3 A_a\,dx^a$, so every $A_a$ is in tesla-metres. Take $\chi\in C^2(U;\mathbb R)$ in webers and a charged test field $\psi\in C^1(U;\mathbb C^N)$, where $N\ge1$ is fixed. With a constant real charge parameter $q$ in coulombs, define $D_a\psi=\partial_a\psi-iqA_a\psi/\hbar$ componentwise. The transformed fields are again $C^1$, with $d\chi=\sum_a(\partial_a\chi)dx^a$. In operator notation the conventions are
$$D_a=\partial_a-\frac{iqA_a}{\hbar},\qquad \psi\mapsto e^{iq\chi/\hbar}\psi,\qquad A\mapsto A+d\chi.$$
For the electron parameter use $q=-e$. The equivalent natural-unit coordinates are $A_{\rm nat}=A_{\rm SI}/\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}$ and $q_{\rm nat}=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$.

Finite-matrix examples act on $\mathbb C^d$ with the operator norm. For Hilbert spaces, use the first-variable-linear pairing $(u,v)_1=v^\dagger u$; a displayed coordinate contraction $u^\dagger v$ is second-variable-linear and equals $\overline{(u,v)_1}$. Thus norms, traces, and modulus-squared amplitudes agree under conversion, although the unsquared pairing is conjugated. No amplitude is assigned a probability by these conventions.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.
